title: Add a single quick retry to IBKRProvider's HTTP requests before failing, given the gateway's demonstrated transient flakiness
description:
Follow-up from a backend-wide IBKR-call-optimization audit this session. Confirmed via reading the current code before writing this task: `IBKRProvider._request` (`backend/app/data/ibkr_provider.py`) raises `IBKRUnavailableError` immediately on the very first failure -- a network error, a non-200 response, or an unparseable JSON body -- with zero retry attempts of any kind.

This is not a hypothetical concern: this very session directly observed the configured IBKR gateway (the same host `IBKRProvider` talks to) flip between unreachable, HTTP 400 ('no bridge'), HTTP 401 (unauthenticated), and 200-authenticated states multiple times within a roughly 20-minute window while working `backend-ibkr-primary-data-provider` -- genuinely transient flakiness, empirically confirmed rather than assumed. A single quick retry (e.g. one retry after a short delay, on the order of 200-500ms) would plausibly absorb a meaningful fraction of these transient failures instead of degrading an entire request (and, per `backend-ibkr-primary-data-provider`'s own design, forcing a 503 with no yfinance/Stooq fallback while IBKR is otherwise connected) over what may just be a momentary blip.

This is a genuinely new finding -- not something previously evaluated or decided against: the existing closed-out IBKR follow-up tasks (`backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups*`, `backend-ibkr-primary-data-provider-followups*`) addressed timeout values, gateway-status caching, and thread-pool nesting, but never retry/backoff behavior on the request layer itself.

checklist.step: Decide and record (decisions entry) the retry policy: how many retries (the description suggests a single quick retry as a reasonable starting point, but confirm against what's actually observed/reasonable), what delay (fixed vs. a short exponential backoff), and which failure types are worth retrying (a network/connection error and a 5xx response are plausible retry candidates; a 401/403 authentication failure or a 4xx client error almost certainly is not, since retrying won't fix those -- read `IBKRProvider._request`'s actual current error-classification logic before deciding exactly where the retry boundary sits).

Implement the retry in `IBKRProvider._request` (or wherever it's cleanest given the function's current structure), being careful not to multiply already-existing timeout/retry effects in any caller that itself has its own retry or timeout wrapper -- check `get_daily_bars`/`get_weekly_bars`/`get_extended_data`'s callers and the per-call timeout (`_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`-equivalent for IBKR, if one exists) to make sure retries don't silently balloon worst-case latency for a caller that's itself running inside a `ThreadPoolExecutor` fan-out with its own deadline expectations.

Tests (no live network calls per Testing.md, mocked IBKR HTTP boundary matching `tests/unit/data/test_ibkr_provider.py`'s existing convention): a transient-failure-then-success case (confirms the retry actually recovers), a persistent-failure case (confirms it still eventually raises `IBKRUnavailableError` after exhausting retries, not an infinite loop), and a non-retryable-error case (confirms a 401/4xx-class failure doesn't get retried per the policy decided above).

decisions.decision: `IBKRProvider._request` now retries exactly once (`_REQUEST_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 2`: the original attempt plus one retry, not an open-ended/exponential-backoff loop) after a fixed `_REQUEST_RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS = 0.3` (300ms) delay, for exactly two failure families: (1) a network/connection-level `httpx.RequestError` that is NOT a `httpx.TimeoutException` (e.g. `ConnectError`/connection-refused -- a fast failure), and (2) an HTTP 5xx response. Explicitly NOT retried: any `httpx.TimeoutException` subtype (`ConnectTimeout`/`ReadTimeout`/`WriteTimeout`/`PoolTimeout`), any HTTP 4xx response (401/403 auth failures, 400 'no bridge', etc.), and an unparseable (non-JSON) 200 body.
decisions.rationale: A single retry rather than more: every gateway flip this session actually observed while working backend-ibkr-primary-data-provider (unreachable -> 400 -> 401 -> 200-authenticated, repeatedly within ~20 minutes) was a fast, binary flip between states, not a slow degradation that might need several attempts to clear -- one retry is already enough to plausibly catch a flip that resolves within a few hundred ms, and a second/third retry would only add latency with no evidence from the observed behavior that it would ever help where the first retry didn't. 300ms (middle of the task description's suggested 200-500ms range): long enough to give a flapping gateway process a moment to settle, short enough that doubling it via one retry stays well under what a caller fanning out several concurrent IBKR calls would notice (see the next entry on the latency-multiplication check). Retrying connection errors and 5xx but not 4xx matches the task description's own reasoning almost exactly -- a 401/403/400 reflects the gateway's current session/request state, which an identical request 300ms later won't change, so retrying it would just waste a round trip and delay the (correct, not-going-to-change) failure response. The one refinement beyond the description's literal wording: `httpx.TimeoutException` is technically a subtype of the generally-retryable `httpx.RequestError` family, but it is deliberately excluded from the retry -- a timeout has already spent this call's full `timeout` budget (default 10s) waiting, so retrying it would silently double a slow failure's already-worst-case latency for a caller with its own timeout/deadline expectations (`app.api.routers.stocks.get_analysis`'s concurrent daily/weekly/extended `ThreadPoolExecutor` fan-out, `app.data.day_trader_intraday`'s per-leg fan-out), which is exactly the 'don't multiply latency effects' risk the task's own checklist item 2 called out, and none of this session's actually-observed flakiness was a timeout in the first place (every flip was an immediate connection refusal or an immediate non-200 response, never a hang). An unparseable 200 body is also excluded: this session never actually observed that failure mode live (unlike the status/connectivity-level flips), and a 200 means the transport layer already succeeded, so retrying it is a materially different (and empirically unmotivated) risk than retrying a connection/5xx failure -- rejected alternative: retry it too for symmetry with the other two original failure modes `_request` already classified, but there is no actual evidence this ever happens against the real gateway, and retrying a nominally-successful response adds a full extra round trip for a hypothetical case.

decisions.decision: Confirmed the retry does not multiply latency for any caller running inside a `ThreadPoolExecutor` fan-out with its own deadline expectations (checklist item 2), and added an injectable `sleep: Callable[[float], None] = time.sleep` constructor parameter (alongside the existing `client`/`clock`) so tests can avoid a real 300ms pause.
decisions.rationale: Traced every concurrent fan-out that can end up calling `IBKRProvider._request`: `app.api.routers.stocks.get_analysis`'s 3-leg `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)` (daily/weekly/extended, each leg independent, no shared deadline enforced across legs beyond each provider's own per-call `httpx` timeout) and `app.data.day_trader_intraday`'s per-leg fan-out -- neither imposes a tighter cross-leg deadline than the sum of each individual IBKR call's own retries, and `get_daily_bars`/`get_weekly_bars`/`resolve_conid` are each a single `_request` call (not already individually retried/looped elsewhere), so the retry's worst-case added cost per leg is exactly one extra `_REQUEST_RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS` (0.3s) plus one extra fast (connection-refused or 5xx) round trip -- not doubled per-call timeouts, since `httpx.TimeoutException` is excluded from the retry (see the policy entry above) specifically to prevent that multiplication. `get_hourly_bars`'s pagination loop (`_MAX_PAGINATION_PAGES = 20`) is the one place a single top-level call can issue many `_request` calls; a worst case of every single page hitting a retryable failure would add `20 * 0.3s = 6s`, but that requires every page to independently fail-then-recover, which is a much rarer compound event than a single call doing so, and the existing 20-page bound was already sized as a safety cap against pathological cases, not a tight latency budget. The injectable `sleep` mirrors the existing `clock` injection pattern (used by the rate-limit tests) rather than inventing a different test-double mechanism, and keeps the new retry tests from actually pausing for 300ms each.

comments.summary: `run_scanner`'s `_request` retry doesn't account for `/iserver/scanner/run`'s own externally-enforced 1-req/sec rate limit (docs/ideas.md, mirrored client-side by `_SCANNER_RUN_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS`). A retryable failure (connection error or 5xx) on that specific endpoint fires a second real HTTP call only `_REQUEST_RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS` (300ms) later -- well inside the 1-second window IBKR's own gateway enforces -- so the retry is plausibly rejected by that same limiter (and risks IBKR-side abuse flagging) rather than recovering. Non-blocking: the worst case is a wasted retry (same eventual failure as without one), not incorrect behavior, and IBKR's exact server-side counting of failed requests against the window is unconfirmed (no live gateway available per this module's own testing constraint). Found by the code-review skill pass.

`get_gateway_status`'s cold-cache path calls `_request("GET", "/iserver/auth/status")` entirely inside `_gateway_status_lock`, so the new retry (up to one extra round trip plus a 300ms sleep) roughly doubles the worst-case time that lock is held -- extending contention for every other thread racing the same cache-miss/expiry (e.g. `get_analysis`'s 3-leg `ThreadPoolExecutor` fan-out, which shares one `IBKRProvider` singleton and hence this one lock) during exactly the gateway-flapping window this retry targets. Non-blocking: the extra delay is shared once across all blocked threads (not multiplied per leg, since double-checked locking means only the first thread pays for the retry), and the task's own decisions entry's headline conclusion (worst case stays sub-second and bounded) still holds -- it just didn't call out this specific shared-lock serialization effect. Found by the code-review skill pass.

The second `decisions` entry's claim that the retry's worst-case added cost is 'exactly one extra `_REQUEST_RETRY_DELAY_SECONDS` (0.3s) plus one extra fast ... round trip' per leg is imprecise for a cold-conid-cache leg in `get_analysis`'s daily/weekly fetches: `IBKRDataProvider.get_daily_ohlcv`/`get_weekly_ohlcv` each issue two sequential `_request` calls (`resolve_conid` via `_resolve_conid_or_raise`, then `get_daily_bars`/`get_weekly_bars`), so an uncached ticker's leg could independently retry both calls, adding up to ~0.6s rather than ~0.3s on that leg. Still small and bounded (and only on a cold `_conid_cache`, which has a 24h TTL), but the written rationale understates it for that specific case. Verified by tracing `resolve_conid`/`get_daily_bars`/`get_weekly_bars` call sites myself during review.

review.notes: Full review: gh pr checkout 383. Backend suite: `pytest --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing` -> 1585 passed, 100% line/branch coverage (matches PR claim). Static analysis: `ruff check .` clean; `mypy --no-incremental app` clean (sandbox auto-mode workaround per dispatch instructions -- plain `mypy`'s incremental-cache write gets blocked as 'Irreversible Local Destruction'). `python3 scripts/validate_tasks.py` -> no violations. Mutation-tested the retry logic myself: (1) set `_REQUEST_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 1` (disables the retry loop) -> the 4 retry-recovery/retry-bound tests in `TestRequestRetry` correctly failed, confirming they actually exercise the retry; (2) removed the `isinstance(exc, httpx.TimeoutException)` guard from the `RequestError` except-branch -> `test_timeout_exception_is_not_retried` correctly failed, confirming that test genuinely catches a timeout-gets-retried regression. Restored the file cleanly after each mutation (`git status --porcelain` empty afterward). Confirmed `httpx.TimeoutException` is a real subclass of `httpx.RequestError` (`issubclass(httpx.TimeoutException, httpx.RequestError) == True`) and that the code's `isinstance` check inside the single `except httpx.RequestError` clause correctly excludes it from retry regardless of except-clause ordering (there's only one except clause here, so the subclass-shadowing concern the dispatch flagged doesn't actually apply -- it's a single catch + explicit isinstance check, not two except clauses that could shadow each other). Traced the latency-multiplication analysis myself: `get_analysis`'s 3-leg fetch (`app/api/routers/stocks.py`, `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)`, all 3 legs submitted/started concurrently) and `day_trader_intraday._fetch_legs_concurrently` (`max_workers=len(legs)`, same concurrent-start pattern) both run their legs in parallel, so the retry's worst-case added latency is bounded by the single slowest leg's own extra delay, not summed across legs -- confirms the decisions entry's headline conclusion, modulo the two precision findings above (scanner rate-limit interaction, shared gateway-status-lock hold time, and my own cold-conid-cache two-call-per-leg nuance). No API route or schema touched (no `backend/openapi.json` staleness concern). Area is `backend/data`, not `backend/signals`/`backend/portfolio`, so `verify-elder-signal` doesn't apply. No new module/dependency/layer added (an injectable `sleep` param mirroring the existing `clock` pattern), so `architecture-review` doesn't apply. No frontend/UI surface touched by this PR (diff is `backend/app/data/ibkr_provider.py`, its test file, and the task board) -- browser walkthrough (step 9) and the persisted e2e suite (step 9a) are explicitly skipped as not applicable. Checklist item 1 ('decide and record the retry policy') has a corresponding, thorough `decisions` entry -- no undocumented judgment call. All three findings above are non-blocking (no correctness bug causing wrong behavior, no coverage regression, no failing test) and are tracked on `docs/tasks/backend-ibkr-request-retry-followups.json`.
